passages.text: and suppliers; (xiv) failure to maintain our credit ratings and potential resulting increases to our cost of borrowing and adverse effects on our cost of funds, liquidity, competitive position and access to capital markets; (xv) our Financial Products segment’s risks associated with the financial services industry; (xvi) changes in interest rates or market liquidity conditions; (xvii) an increase in delinquencies, repossessions or net losses of Cat Financial’s customers; (xviii) currency fluctuations; (xix) our or Cat Financial’s compliance with financial and other restrictive covenants in debt agreements; (xx) increased pension plan funding obligations; (xxi) alleged or actual violations of trade or anti-corruption laws and regulations; (xxii) additional tax expense or exposure, including the impact of U.S. tax reform; (xxiii) significant legal proceedings, claims, lawsuits or government investigations; (xxiv) new regulations or changes in financial services regulations; (xxv) compliance with environmental laws and regulations; (xxvi) catastrophic events, including global pandemics such as the COVID-19 pandemic; and (xxvii) other factors described in more detail in Caterpillar’s Forms 10-Q, 10-K and other filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Welcome to the Third Quarter 2026 Caterpillar Earnings Conference Call. Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your speaker today, Alex Kapper. Thank you. Please go ahead.

passages.heading: Alex Kapper, Vice President of Investor Relations
passages.text: Alex Kapper, Vice President of Investor Relations: Thank you, Audra. Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Caterpillar's Third Quarter of 2026 Earnings Call. I'm Alex Kapper, Vice President of Investor Relations. Joining me today are Joe Creed, Chairman and CEO; Kyle Epley, Chief Financial Officer; Stephanie Baughman, Senior Vice President of the Global Finance Services Division; and Ryan Coleman, Senior Director of IR. During our call, we'll be discussing the third quarter earnings release we issued earlier today. You can find our slides, the news release, and a webcast recap at investors.caterpillar.com under Events and Presentations. The content of this call is protected by U.S. and international copyright law. Any rebroadcast, retransmission, reproduction, or distribution of all or part of this content without Caterpillar's prior written permission is prohibited. Moving to Slide 2. During our call today, we'll make forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. We'll also make assumptions that could cause our actual results to be different than the information we're sharing with you on this call. Please refer to our recent SEC filings, the forward-looking statements reminder, and the news release for details on factors that individually or in aggregate could cause our actual results to vary materially from our forecast. A detailed discussion of the many factors that we believe may have a material effect on our business on an ongoing basis is

passages.heading: Alex Kapper, Vice President of Investor Relations
passages.text: contained in our SEC filings. On today's call, we'll also refer to non-GAAP numbers. For any reconciliation of non-GAAP numbers to the appropriate U.S. GAAP numbers, please see the appendix of the earnings call slides. For today's agenda, Joe will begin by sharing his perspectives about our results, and he will highlight key initiatives across our segments. Then he'll discuss our full-year outlook and insights about our end markets. Kyle will provide a detailed overview of results and share key assumptions looking forward. We will conclude by taking your questions. Now let's advance to Slide 3 and turn the call over to Joe Creed.

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO: All right. Good morning, and thanks, Alex. I appreciate everyone joining us today. Our third-quarter results reflect the durability of our end markets, with our highest sales quarter ever, strong order rates, and a record backlog. Our team continues to execute our strategic priorities in a dynamic environment, positioning us for a strong year. Sales and revenues were $20.7 billion, up 17% versus the prior year, driven by strong end-market demand. We delivered adjusted profit per share of $7.20, an increase of 45% versus last year. Strong order rates across all three of our primary segments drove backlog to a record $78 billion. That's an increase of approximately $38 billion, or 96%, from the third quarter last year and marks the fourth consecutive quarter of sequential backlog growth in all three of our primary segments. The quarter demonstrated the team's ability to execute in a high-growth environment. Specifically, our Power and Energy team continued to increase production of large reciprocating engines and turbines while simultaneously expanding capacity to meet demand. The team is effectively managing the operational challenges that come with this rapid growth. Bringing additional capacity online is still the top pacing factor for growth in Power and Energy, so we're working diligently to execute our plans and meet our customers' needs. As I mentioned, sales and revenues were $20.7 billion, and they were in line with our expectations.

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: The increase from the prior year was primarily driven by strong growth in sales volume and favorable price realization in all three of our primary segments. Third-quarter adjusted operating profit margin was 20.6%. Excluding IEEPA tariff recoveries, adjusted operating profit margin was in line with our expectations. In the third quarter, we generated MP&E free cash flow of $3.8 billion and deployed $2 billion to shareholders through share repurchases and dividends. Now I'll review third-quarter retail statistics. In Power and Energy, sales to users grew a robust 36%. Power generation grew 75%, driven by continued very strong demand for turbines and large reciprocating engines used in data center applications. Sales to users in oil and gas increased 5% and were driven by turbines and turbine-related services. Industrial sales to users were down due to softness in the EAME region. Now for Construction Industries. We have one of the broadest ranges of products, technology, and services to support customers, whether they prefer to own, lease, or rent equipment. Combined with healthy construction activity, our unique position has allowed us to outpace the industry throughout the year. In the third quarter, total sales to users increased 20%, marking the seventh consecutive quarter of year-over-year growth. In North America, sales to users grew a robust 27%, in line with our expectations. Dealer rental revenue in North America continued to grow, driving increased investment in

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: their equipment fleets. We also saw strong customer interest in the Cat dealer-owned rental joint venture called Major Projects, which was launched last quarter. As a reminder, Major Projects will serve customers developing large-scale infrastructure across North America, including transportation, energy, manufacturing, and data center builds. It's a supplemental national rental solution to help deliver larger-size-class construction equipment and capabilities where existing individual dealer rental fleets aren't sufficient to execute at scale. As a result, rental fleet loading was exceptionally strong in the third quarter, contributing significantly to sales-to-users growth compared with the prior year, when fleet loading was a slight headwind. Even excluding the positive impact from rental fleet loading, sales-to-users growth was strong, driven by residential and nonresidential construction activity. Sales to users in EAME were above expectations, with growth driven by strength in Europe and Africa, partially offset by softness in the Middle East. In Asia Pacific, sales to users outside of China were lower than we anticipated and declined slightly due to timing. China, however, continued to grow from a low base as we expected. Latin America continued to grow but at a lower rate than we anticipated. For Resource Industries, third-quarter sales to users increased 4%, which is below our expectations. Sales to users were higher in heavy construction, quarry, and aggregates,

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: but lower in mining due to delays in shipping and commissioning. The rail decrease was driven by lower international locomotive deliveries. Turning to Slide 4. I'll cover a few highlights since our last earnings call, starting with Power and Energy. We serve customers across the power and energy value chain, and demand for our solutions remains strong. To ensure we can meet their needs and maintain operational excellence, we're continually evaluating opportunities to repurpose underutilized facilities across our footprint. In line with that approach, we plan to use a portion of our Winston-Salem, North Carolina facility, which currently produces locomotive engines, as a second assembly and test location for the 3600 series large reciprocating engine. The footprint will support our oil and gas customers to meet the growing need for natural gas compression. The initiative directly supports previously announced plans to increase large reciprocating engine capacity to nearly three times the 2024 level by 2030. Utilizing our existing footprint and workforce is the most cost-effective and quickest way for us to bring additional capacity online. In Construction Industries, we launched Cat Compact earlier this year, a key part of our strategy to reach more small contractors in the growing compact construction equipment industry. To support that growth and meet increasing customer demand, we announced a $1 billion investment to expand manufacturing capacity in Sanford, North

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: Carolina. The investment will create a modern, technology-enabled manufacturing environment designed to improve safety, quality, and operational performance while supporting long-term growth. The facility will incorporate advanced manufacturing technologies, automation, digital production systems, and integrated logistics capabilities to create a more connected and efficient operation. This demonstrates how we're aligning our investments to meet our 2030 targets and positioning Caterpillar for long-term profitable growth. And in Resource Industries, we announced last month that we're working with Luck Stone to expand autonomous hauling technology across two additional Virginia operations. The expansion follows a highly successful pilot at the Bull Run quarry, where autonomous trucks have hauled more than 3.5 million tons since going live in November 2024. These deployments also marked the first use of Caterpillar's autonomous technology on a Cat 775 truck, expanding our advanced autonomy capabilities beyond large mining applications and into quarry and aggregates. Through this customer collaboration, we gained insights that are helping us refine and scale our autonomous hauling solutions to deliver measurable value for operations at job sites around the world. This expansion marks another important step toward our goal of tripling the number of Cat autonomous trucks by 2030 compared with 2024. Now on Slide 5, I'll provide an update on our outlook. Our strong execution

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: through the first nine months positions us well to meet our full-year outlook. We continue to expect our full-year 2026 sales and revenues to grow in the mid- to high teens. Strong order rates and a growing backlog reflect continued broad-based momentum across our business despite ongoing geopolitical uncertainty. Excluding the favorable impact from IEEPA tariff recoveries, we continue to expect full-year adjusted operating profit margin to be near the bottom of the target range. Our full-year margin expectation reflects the strategic investments we're making to execute our growth strategy, as well as the ongoing impact of tariffs and higher freight costs due to elevated energy prices. We remain focused on delivering long-term OPACC growth, and we aim to operate around the midpoint of our adjusted operating profit margin target range over time. We're also maintaining our MP&E free cash flow expectations to be in the top half of our annual target range. Kyle will provide additional details shortly. And now I'll discuss our key end markets, starting with Power and Energy. We continue to work closely with our customers, which allows us to understand and respond to their evolving needs. Customers' view of demand for both oil and gas and power generation remains strong. As I mentioned, backlog continues to grow due to strong order rates, and we're now taking some large reciprocating orders as far out as 2029 and turbine orders into 2030. We continue to anticipate full-year

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: growth in power generation for both Cat reciprocating engines and Solar Turbines, driven by increasing energy demand to support the data center build-out related to cloud computing and generative AI. Additionally, prime power demand continues to trend higher as customers look to Caterpillar's turbine and reciprocating engine products to support their need for power solutions. After a record year for sales in 2025, oil and gas is expected to grow moderately again this year. Reciprocating engine sales are anticipated to increase, driven by strong demand in gas compression applications. We also see continued momentum in demand for reciprocating engine aftermarket parts. Solar Turbines oil and gas sales are expected to grow, and the backlog remains healthy with solid order and inquiry activity. Demand for products in industrial applications is expected to grow moderately in 2026 as well. For Construction Industries, we expect strong fourth-quarter and full-year sales-to-users growth, supported by healthy end markets. The outlook for North America remains positive, with construction spending at healthy levels. Nonresidential construction investment continues to be supported by the IIJA, critical infrastructure programs, and data centers. We expect fourth-quarter dealer rental fleet loading to remain strong. However, it will contribute less to sales-to-users growth than in the third quarter due to lapping strong rental loading in the fourth quarter of last year. In EAME, Europe

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: is expected to remain stable, supported by nonresidential construction, while construction activity in Africa is projected to remain strong. The Middle East continues to face challenges, and we currently anticipate only a limited impact on EAME sales to users. In Asia Pacific, outside of China, stable economic conditions are expected. In China, we anticipate moderate conditions, with full-year growth in the above-10-ton excavator industry off low levels of activity. We expect full-year growth in Latin America. We're seeing continued positive momentum in Resource Industries, with robust order rates driving strong backlog growth. Customer product utilization is high, and the age of the fleet remains elevated. Most key commodities remain above investment thresholds, and customers are focused on the long term. For full-year 2026, we expect strong sales-to-users growth, primarily driven by rising demand for copper and gold, increasing activity in the Canadian oil sands, and positive dynamics in heavy construction and quarry and aggregates. We expect commissioning delays from the third quarter to catch up, which will contribute to strong sales-to-users growth in the fourth quarter. We continue to expect rebuild activity to increase moderately compared with last year. Rail services are anticipated to grow for the year, and we now expect locomotive deliveries to be slightly lower year over year due to timing of deliveries. And finally, earlier this month, we announced that Derrick

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: York will succeed Denise Johnson as Group President of Resource Industries. I want to congratulate Denise on a remarkable career. Under her leadership, Resource Industries returned to profitability and positioned Caterpillar as an industry leader in mining, autonomy, and technology. I'm deeply grateful for all she's done to strengthen our relationships with customers, develop our people, and shape the future of our company. Her impact and influence will be remembered long after her retirement. I've worked closely with Derrick for well over a decade, and I'm confident in his ability to lead the RI team into its next chapter of innovation, growth, and customer success. He is a highly respected leader who understands our customers, our strategy, and the industries that we serve. With that, I'll turn it over to Kyle.

passages.heading: Kyle Epley, Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Kyle Epley, Chief Financial Officer: Thank you, Joe. Good morning, everyone. I'm going to take a few minutes to walk you through our third-quarter results, including details about segment performance as well as the balance sheet and cash flow. I will finish with remarks on our expectations for the fourth quarter and current full-year assumptions. Beginning on Slide 6. Sales and revenues were $20.7 billion, up 17% versus the prior year, which was in line with our expectations. Adjusted operating profit was $4.3 billion, and our adjusted operating profit margin was 20.6%. Excluding the IEEPA tariff recoveries, both were in line with expectations. Moving to Slide 7, the 17% increase in sales and revenues compared to the third quarter of 2025 was primarily driven by strong growth in sales volume and favorable price realization. The stronger sales volume was mainly driven by higher sales of equipment to end users, supported by healthy end-market demand and strong execution by our team. Dealer inventory increased by $300 million in Construction Industries compared to an increase of $600 million in the third quarter of 2025. This created a modest headwind to sales volume in the quarter and was in line with our expectations. Sales and revenues, both at a consolidated level and across all three primary segments, were in line with our expectations. Moving to operating profit on Slide 8. Operating profit in the third quarter increased by 38% to $4.2 billion. Adjusted operating profit

passages.heading: Kyle Epley, Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: of $4.3 billion also increased by 38% versus the prior year. The adjusted operating profit margin was 20.6%, an increase of 310 basis points compared to the prior year. The margin benefited from the profit impact of higher sales volume and favorable price realization. This was partially offset by higher manufacturing costs, mainly driven by higher freight and higher expenses related to our capacity expansions. In the quarter, we recognized $128 million in IEEPA tariff recoveries. Nearly all this amount is reflected in corporate items. For tariffs introduced since the beginning of 2025 and excluding IEEPA recoveries, our third-quarter tariff costs were approximately $600 million and about flat year over year, as we anticipated. Moving to Slide 9. Profit per share was $7.13 in the quarter. Adjusted profit per share was $7.20. Excluding discrete items, the provision for income taxes in the third quarter of 2026 reflected a global estimated annual effective tax rate of 23%. Finally, the year-over-year impact from the reduction in the average number of shares outstanding due to share repurchases resulted in a favorable impact on adjusted profit per share of approximately $0.15 compared to the third quarter of 2025. On Slide 10, I will now review the third-quarter results of our segments, starting with Power and Energy. For Power and Energy, sales of $8.8 billion increased by 18% versus the prior year, which was in line with our expectations. The sales increase versus the prior

passages.heading: Kyle Epley, Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: year was mainly due to higher sales volume and favorable price realization. Services revenues were also strong in the quarter, especially for sales into oil and gas applications. Third-quarter profit for Power and Energy increased by 31% versus the prior year to $2.1 billion. The segment's margin of 24.4% was an increase of 250 basis points versus the prior year. The increase was mainly due to the profit impact of higher sales volume. Favorable price realization was mostly offset by unfavorable manufacturing costs driven by spend related to our capacity expansions, including higher depreciation, along with higher freight and material costs. Segment margins matched our expectations. Now moving to Slide 11. Construction Industries sales increased by 18% in the third quarter to $8 billion, as we anticipated. The sales increase versus the prior year was primarily due to higher sales volume and favorable price realization. Higher sales volume was mainly driven by sales of equipment to end users, which included strong contributions from both retail sales and rental fleet loading. Both residential and nonresidential industries contributed to the growth. Third-quarter profit for Construction Industries was $1.8 billion, a 33% increase versus the prior year. The segment's margin of 22.9% was an increase of 250 basis points versus the prior year, mainly driven by favorable price realization and the profit impact of higher sales volume. This was partially offset by unfavorable

passages.heading: Kyle Epley, Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: manufacturing costs, including the impact of freight and tariff costs. SG&A and R&D expenses related to our digital and technology investments also increased compared to the prior year. Segment margin was also consistent with our expectations. Turning to Slide 12. Resource Industries sales, which were broadly in line with our expectations, increased by 15% in the third quarter to $4.6 billion, primarily driven by higher sales volume. Price realization was also favorable versus the prior year and slightly better than our expectations, primarily driven by positive geographic mix. Third-quarter profit for Resource Industries increased by 14% versus the prior year to $622 million. The segment's margin of 13.5% was roughly unchanged versus the prior year. This was mainly driven by unfavorable manufacturing costs, primarily due to higher material costs, including tariffs, offset by the profit impact of higher sales volume and favorable price realization. Overall, the segment margin was about in line with our expectations. Moving to Slide 13. Financial Products revenues increased by 9% versus the prior year to $1.2 billion, mainly due to higher average earning assets across all regions. Segment profit increased by 10% to $264 million. This increase was primarily due to a favorable impact from higher average earning assets, partially offset by a higher provision for credit losses. Our customers' financial health remains strong. Past dues were 1.31% in the quarter, down 16 basis

passages.heading: Kyle Epley, Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: points versus the prior year, and remain the lowest level we have recorded since 1998. The allowance rate was 0.91% at the end of the third quarter. Business activity within Cat Financial remains healthy. Retail new business volume grew by 6% versus the prior year. In addition, used equipment inventory levels continue to remain low, and conversion rates remain above historical averages as customers continue to choose to purchase their equipment at the end of their lease term. Moving on to Slide 14. MP&E free cash flow was $3.8 billion in the quarter. This was an increase of roughly $600 million versus the prior year, mainly driven by stronger profit. CapEx spend was about $700 million in the quarter. We deployed $2 billion to shareholders in the third quarter, of which share repurchases accounted for $1.2 billion and nearly $750 million for our quarterly dividend payment. Earlier this year, we announced our sixth consecutive year of a high-single-digit quarterly dividend increase, and this year will mark 33 consecutive years of paying higher annual dividends to our shareholders. Our balance sheet remains strong. We have ample liquidity with an enterprise cash balance of $7.9 billion. In addition, there is $1.6 billion in slightly longer-dated liquid marketable securities to improve yields on our cash. Now for outlook assumptions. Turning to Slide 15. I will start with the fourth quarter. End-user demand remains favorable across all three primary segments, and the team is

passages.heading: Kyle Epley, Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: working diligently to deliver on our commitments for the year. At the same time, we are aware of potential headwinds presented by higher cost inflation, which we continue to monitor closely. For the fourth quarter, we anticipate moderate sales growth versus the prior year. As a reminder, we are lapping a strong quarter last year, which creates a tougher comparison this year. Now let me walk you through each of our three primary segments. In Power and Energy, we anticipate moderate sales growth in the fourth quarter versus the prior year as we lap a strong prior-year fourth quarter and continue to ramp capacity. Volume growth is expected to be driven by continued strength in power generation, modest growth in oil and gas, and moderate growth in industrial applications as it continues to recover. We also expect favorable price realization. In Construction Industries, we expect sales to be similar to the prior year. We anticipate the typical seasonal dealer inventory reduction to be roughly $1.6 billion, which compares to a decline of $600 million in the fourth quarter of 2025. As a result, we expect the year-over-year impact to be about a $1 billion headwind to sales volume in the fourth quarter against the backdrop of continued strong sales to users and industry growth. As a result, we expect sales volume in Construction Industries to be down modestly versus the prior year. However, we continue to expect favorable price realization in the fourth quarter. Despite the

passages.heading: Kyle Epley, Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: drawdown, we continue to expect dealer inventories at the end of the year to be higher than the prior year in anticipation of strong sales to users in 2027. In Resource Industries, we expect strong sales growth in the fourth quarter versus the prior year. Volume is expected to be driven by higher sales to users and services growth. We also anticipate favorable price realization. I will now provide some color on our fourth-quarter margin expectations versus the prior year. At the enterprise level, we expect higher adjusted operating profit margin versus the prior year. This is primarily due to favorable price realization and the profit impact of higher sales volume. Excluding the impact of lower tariffs, we expect unfavorable manufacturing costs driven by higher freight as well as expenses related to our capacity expansions. SG&A and R&D expenses are also expected to be higher, driven by our continued investment in the strategic initiatives aligned with our 2030 goals. We anticipate tariff costs, excluding IEEPA recoveries, of around $600 million, which is similar to what we incurred in the third quarter, but roughly $200 million lower than what we incurred in the fourth quarter of 2025. We continue to expect about 50% of the tariffs to be incurred in Construction Industries and 25% in both Power and Energy and Resource Industries. Now for our fourth-quarter margin expectations in our three primary segments. In Power and Energy, we anticipate favorable price realization and

passages.heading: Kyle Epley, Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: stronger volume to drive a higher margin percentage compared to the prior year. The higher margin compared to the prior year is expected to be partially offset by unfavorable manufacturing costs, including depreciation and expenses related to our capacity expansion, along with higher material and freight costs. We expect fourth-quarter margin to be similar to the third quarter. In Construction Industries, we anticipate a higher margin percentage compared to the prior year, primarily due to favorable price realization, which is partially offset by lower sales volume. Excluding the impact of lower tariffs, manufacturing costs are expected to be higher, driven by freight. We also expect higher SG&A and R&D related to our technology investments. Also, as a reminder, our Construction Industries fourth-quarter margin typically has a sequential step-down from the third quarter. We expect this seasonality change to be slightly more than our typical average step-down due to the expected lower sales volume, higher SG&A and R&D related to our technology and digital investments, as well as higher freight costs. In Resource Industries, we anticipate a higher margin percentage compared to the prior year, driven by favorable price realization and the profit impact of higher sales volume, partially offset by unfavorable manufacturing costs, including freight and material. Now on Slide 16, let me provide a few comments on the full year. As Joe mentioned, we continue to anticipate sales and

passages.heading: Kyle Epley, Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: revenues growth in the mid- to high teens for full-year 2026. Our strong full-year sales and revenues expectations are supported by strong sales-to-users growth across all three primary segments, driven by healthy end markets; strong order rates across all three primary segments driving our backlog growth; increased output from our capacity expansion plans, which remain on schedule; and a strong year of services growth. Now for our adjusted operating profit margin for the full year. Compared to last year, we expect a higher adjusted operating profit margin, which reflects the profit impact of higher sales and favorable price realization, partially offset by unfavorable manufacturing costs, including spend related to our capacity expansion, which includes higher depreciation expense as well as higher freight. We also expect higher SG&A and R&D. Excluding IEEPA tariff recoveries, our full-year adjusted operating profit margin is expected to be near the bottom of our target range. Excluding our reported year-to-date IEEPA tariff recoveries of about $520 million, we continue to expect full-year 2026 tariff costs of around $2.2 billion. Our outlook does not include any additional IEEPA tariff recoveries in the fourth quarter. We now expect restructuring costs of about $300 million in 2026, which is on the low end of our prior range. Our estimated global annual effective tax rate remains approximately 23% for 2026, excluding discrete items. We also continue to expect MP&E free

passages.heading: Kyle Epley, Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: cash flow to be in the top half of our annual target range of $6 billion to $15 billion. Our CapEx spend for 2026 is now anticipated to be about $3.3 billion, which is slightly below our prior expectations of $3.5 billion. Now turning to Slide 17 to summarize. We delivered another very strong quarter, with year-to-date financial results tracking toward another record year for Caterpillar. Our end markets remain healthy with strong order rates and a growing backlog. We continue to drive improved profitability in a dynamic operating environment. We will remain disciplined and committed to operational excellence and the O&E model. We will continue to look for ways to invest efficiently. We will maintain a strong balance sheet and continue to return substantially all of our MP&E free cash flow to our shareholders through dividends and share repurchases over time. And finally, we will continue to execute our strategy for profitable growth. With that, we will take your questions.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Your first question comes from Tami Zakaria from JPMorgan. Hearing no response, we'll go next to Rob Wertheimer with Melius Research.

passages.heading: Robert Wertheimer, Analyst, Melius Research
passages.text: Robert Wertheimer, Analyst, Melius Research: I had a couple of questions around Power Gen. Two quarters ago, you detailed some of the Prime Power projects you've done. I think you gave gigawatt numbers. Do you have any update there? Is Prime Power still expanding for you, either in general or if you have any update on gigawatts? And then you mentioned you're taking orders into '29. Does that imply that '28 is sold out? Are you selling out current capacity but leaving future capacity for future orders? Can you just sort of talk about how you manage backlog there?

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO: Rob, we still continue to see Prime Power trending higher, both turbines and reciprocating gensets. I've had a handful of discussions with customers for Prime Power just in this last quarter. So a lot of quoting activity continues to go on, and I think we'll continue to see that trend as we move into the future. We're not seeing anything different in that space. When it comes to orders and sort of backlog, if it's a significant order in gas, Prime Power, we're probably looking at 2029. I mean, maybe some—we'll probably still roll some diesel backup orders into 2028; we're not completely full. But we still have frame agreements in the pipeline that kind of convert to orders as we move over time. So again, we continue to have extended backlog. I'm happy that the backlog grew in all three segments. And what we're hearing from our customers is they still want more from us if we can get them more power. So we're trying to ramp as quickly as we can and still hit our customers' needs.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: We'll go next to Tami Zakaria at JPMorgan.

passages.heading: Tami Zakaria, Analyst, JPMorgan
passages.text: Tami Zakaria, Analyst, JPMorgan: Good morning. Can you hear me?

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO: We can.

passages.heading: Tami Zakaria, Analyst, JPMorgan
passages.text: Tami Zakaria, Analyst, JPMorgan: So just wanted to touch on that backlog comment. I think I heard you say that the engine and turbine orders are now going as far as 2029, 2030. So is it that the total orders you received in the quarter are primarily for the out years? Or are the majority of the orders booked still for the next 12 months? And given the new capacity that will be coming online, when would you expect this record backlog to start stepping down? Or is it the new normal for the backlog magnitude?

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO: Tami, thanks for the question. So I want to be clear: we're taking our orders into '29. We have some in '29 and 2030; we still have more to fill. And this is a bit of a complicated question because it's going to depend on the product, right? So for large reciprocating engines and turbines, we're definitely extended out into late '28 into '29. Smaller gensets, smaller engines, obviously, lead times are much shorter than that. And on the machine side of the business, the backlog grew in all three segments, aside from a couple of products where we're ramping production and operationally trying to ramp production, and even those were not extended nearly as far. I would like to produce and get our production ramp closer to STU. So when we look at the backlog, we want to make sure we're looking at the backlog in the context of sales to users and order rates and the entire system and how it works. So if sales to users stay healthy, which is what we're expecting, and we can produce more product, we'll continue to take orders. But I would like to see the backlog—I mean, if we can get it to even come in on the machine side because we can keep up, that would be a good thing. And I also think if you look at it, we've had a few quarters of backlog growth. I think we'll continue to see some backlog growth, but it's going to really depend. I mean, customers have time to place orders and sort of digest what we have. And so I don't know that quarter-to-quarter

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: it's going to be something we look at as the singular metric as we start to move out, especially as we get extended. We're continuing to do long-term planning with our big data center customers and Prime Power customers. We're seeing demand for cloud compute and our backup power continue to be strong. And then AI obviously comes in on top of that in the Prime Power numbers. So with those frame agreements, we have a line of sight past the backlog, and we continue to talk to our customers. And then on Prime Power, those are big projects. And I think they get negotiated individually, and those can come in lumpy in the backlog, as can mining orders. So I'm really pleased with the backlog growth we saw in this quarter. It was broad-based: oil and gas, power gen, RI, and CI. So we have good momentum.

passages.heading: Kyle Epley, Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Kyle Epley, Chief Financial Officer: And just for reference, we expect 58% of our backlog to be sold within the next 12 months, and that's comparative to 59% last quarter.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: We'll move next to Jamie Cook at Truist Securities.

passages.heading: Jamie Cook, Analyst, Truist Securities
passages.text: Jamie Cook, Analyst, Truist Securities: I guess my question, Joe, is just around your longer-term margin framework that you guys have put out there. You guys have done an exceptional job, but the margins have been pushing toward the lower end. Obviously, we have tariffs and inflationary pressures, et cetera. But what do you think, with capacity coming online and price-cost in your backlog, is a reasonable time for us to assume we can get back toward the mid- to high end of your longer-term target range, and what would be the major drivers behind that? And then, lastly, is there any way you can help us frame how much incremental capacity is coming online in 2027 on a dollar basis, or any way you could frame it?

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO: Jamie, as far as the margin target range, I've said many times, I want to operate toward the middle of that range. The sales are growing at a really good clip, which is a good thing, and we've been able to, as best we can, keep up with customer demand. And it's a progressive target, so as our margins are going up, the target continues to increase. So we're kind of skipping along the bottom. I would expect—and we'll talk to you a lot more about 2027 in the next quarter—that we start to claw our way off the bottom of that margin target range as we go forward, while we still try to keep up with demand. We also are trying to do this with the tariff headwind in a smart way, where we're not slowing down investments that would impact the growth and the momentum we have in the business. So I'm happy with the progress we've made. Our margins continue to go up as our volume goes up, and over the next couple of years, we want to try to work our way back to the midpoint.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Next, we'll move to David Raso at Evercore ISI.

passages.heading: David Raso, Analyst, Evercore ISI
passages.text: David Raso, Analyst, Evercore ISI: I'm trying to figure out the revenue sequentially and what it means when we think about '27 revenue. If you look at the sequential revenue, third quarter to fourth quarter, let's use the guide for the full year, mid- to high teens, right? Let's call it 17%. It implies the fourth quarter, even if I give you back the extra $1 billion, right, the headwind of the dealer inventory, it implies the revenue is barely up sequentially. And over a long period of time, fourth quarter is up 5% to 10%. I mean, it moves around, but a year where you're adding capacity—it's a big focus. And demand is there. You speak to retail, even the backlog is still pretty solid. Just trying to understand, is there some capacity issue, supplier issue? Why is the revenue growth so modest sequentially, especially given the capacity adds? And any implications on how to think about '27 top line would be appreciated as well.

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO: As we said in the prepared remarks, on Power and Energy, it's really paced by capacity and timing of customer deliveries. So we're not seeing anything different in the business that we would say would impact the fourth quarter, but it is hand to mouth, right? The teams are working really hard. We had a test cell go down for a little bit in the third quarter that we were able to overcome, but there's no slack in the system. And then, as you mentioned, we've kind of said we're going to have the inventory drawdown in CI, which seasonally isn't unusual. It's going to be a little different than the patterns that we had last year. And then RI, as we mentioned, we think operationally we're trying to ramp. So we're going to obviously get as much product out as we can on large mining trucks and some of those products. But I don't think there's anything other than typical seasonality and things that we've talked about on trying to ramp production. We're pretty confident. And this is in line—our third-quarter results came in line with what we expected. We haven't really changed our view for what we plan to do in the fourth quarter. And as you think about how we're going to finish the year, again, we'll talk to you more about 2027 in January, but our backlog continues to increase. We have a longer line of sight. We are drawing down CI inventory, $1.6 billion. We're going to finish the year with almost $700 million more inventory in place than we finished

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: 2025 heading into 2026. So we feel good about where we sit right now.

passages.heading: Kyle Epley, Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Kyle Epley, Chief Financial Officer: And David, I just—this is Kyle. Just to remind you, as I said in my prepared remarks, when we talk about the growth, it's off a really tough comparison versus fourth quarter last year, just from a consolidated level and then especially from a Power and Energy standpoint. But going into 2027, with the dealer inventory increase in CI, we still expect really strong STUs across all three primary segments in the fourth quarter going into 2027.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: We'll take our next question from Michael Feniger at Bank of America.

passages.heading: Michael Feniger, Analyst, Bank of America
passages.text: Michael Feniger, Analyst, Bank of America: And just kind of following up on David Raso's question. On the fourth quarter implying moderate sales growth, you guys talked about the dealer destock. I know your target is 6% to 9% CAGR on the revenue growth side, some years higher, some years lower to get to that average. Just with the backlog where it is, the framework agreements, and I understand there's a quarter dynamic with destocking, why would you set up for '27—should we be thinking that we're above that 6% to 9% CAGR, at the higher end, based on where retail sales are and what we're seeing? What would hold us back from being in that line? I'm just kind of curious what the setup and the building blocks would look like for next year on that.

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO: Yes. So 2027, again, we don't have much different than how I answered David's question, right? I mean, we're finishing the year strong. As Kyle mentioned, we had a really strong fourth quarter last year. So when we say moderate growth year over year, some of that's a comp issue. Based on capacity in Power and Energy, we think we'll continue to increase capacity. It's not a cliff event, as we've said, so every quarter we try to get more and more product out. We expect to continue that. When it comes to the dealer inventory drawdown, dealers are independent businesses, just to remind you. We do work with them, and we want to make sure we have the right inventory in the right place, in the right regions of the world, with the right products. And we do feel like we're in a good position heading into 2027, finishing the year with more dealer inventory in CI than we finished last year. RI orders continue to go up. We've had three really strong quarters in a row of orders in RI. We're having some operational challenges and inefficiencies as we ramp, but I think we'll continue to work those and get those behind us. So we're pretty confident and bullish in where we sit right now as we watch things. We're focused on delivering a strong fourth quarter and a strong finish to the year, and we'll talk to you guys more about '27 in January.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Next, we'll go to Chad Dillard at Bernstein.

passages.heading: Charles Albert Dillard, Analyst, Bernstein
passages.text: Charles Albert Dillard, Analyst, Bernstein: I just wanted to spend some time on the mining business. I recall from the beginning of this year, you talked about orders being the highest, I think, since 2012. So I was wondering if you could give an update on how that's trending, talk about what's driving it—more refurbishment versus replacement? And if you can just give a little bit more color on some of the ramping challenges that you're seeing? And do you have a line of sight to seeing that being resolved in the next quarter or so?

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO: Yes, we've had three really good order quarters in a row for RI, which we're really happy about. As I mentioned in the prepared remarks, it's driven a lot by mining and heavy construction. But in mining, in particular, copper and gold. We're starting to see activity in the Canadian oil sands. Services are continuing to grow, so customers are using the fleet, and we're seeing aftermarket rebuilds continue to happen and customers are starting to order equipment. So that's all a really good sign. As we try to ramp, particularly in large mining trucks, that's where we've actually been increasing capacity at some of our factories where we can inside our four walls and working with the supply base to get ramped up. There are, I would say, normal growing pains and operational challenges when you're increasing capacity and trying to get product out the door. So we'll continue to work through those. I think we'll get them behind us as we move forward. But it's a great sign that we've had strength in orders as we've been waiting for orders to kind of pick up in mining for quite a while. So we're really happy with what we've seen in the first three quarters of this year.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: We'll go next to Jerry Revich at Wells Fargo Securities.

passages.heading: Jerry Revich, Analyst, Wells Fargo Securities
passages.text: Jerry Revich, Analyst, Wells Fargo Securities: Congratulations to Denise and Derrick. Joe, Kyle, I want to ask, as you think about the production slots and lead times out to '29, '30 for turbines and large reciprocating engines, as you folks look at the permit requirements out there and the counterparty has given some angst about credit in the market, can you just talk about if you've seen any shifts in timing in backlog? And I don't know if you can share what proportion of those production slots are backed by hyperscalers, just to build comfort around the moving pieces given all of the news on the permitting side?

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO: Yes. I mean, I don't think we would quantify hyperscalers versus colos versus others or IPPs, but we work with all of them. Typically, when we roll orders from pipeline into the backlog and work with other customers, we generally have line of sight to the project that they're working on. Our teams are working closely with customers. We continue to see strong oil and gas activity as well for large engines. So as we think of this, we've always tended to move, if we can, some slots around to meet customer needs and deliver on their projects. We've been doing that in the last couple of years because we want to make sure we meet our customers' timelines, but there's no need to get product that early. It allows us to meet more customer demand if we're getting it when they need it. And we haven't seen really any significant change in how we're working with our customers to deliver projects and product to meet their project timelines. So we continue to talk to our customers. We stay close to them. We'll follow their lead, but we're not seeing significant changes. But as I said earlier, as we're extended pretty far out, this is going to be unusual for us. Typically, we only had 12 months or less line of sight to our backlog. And now, particularly in this situation, customers are placing orders pretty far out there. We have a lot of quoting activity in '29, '30. We've had some quoting activity even beyond that as we talk to customers. But I think they

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: have time to firm up those orders and place the firm orders and move them into our backlog. So we'll see our backlog kind of move in a lumpy way moving forward. But we'll continue to watch sales to users. We continue to watch order rates and our backlog, all in conjunction together, and stay close to our customers as we move into the end of this year and into next year.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: We'll move to our next question from Mig Dobre at Baird.

passages.heading: Mircea Dobre, Analyst, Baird
passages.text: Mircea Dobre, Analyst, Baird: Yes. And just to follow up on these last comments, if we're looking at backlog progression or maybe looking at it from the perspective of book-to-bill, it was as high as 1.7 earlier this year and decelerated to about 1.3 in a quarter here. As you look at the fourth quarter, based on what you know, how should we think about book-to-bill here? And given that you're taking orders into '29, maybe even '30 for Solar, is there some kind of slippage in terms of bookings, given how constrained from a capacity standpoint we seem to be?

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO: Yes. I mean, one of the things you have to look at with book-to-bill is that we continue to increase production as well. So our sales are continuing to go up. And as I mentioned, when you look at our backlog, all three segments are in there, and all three have been growing. There are some products where we'd actually like to bring in and increase production. And so as we continue to ramp, book-to-bill will sort of move around. And then in Power and Energy, again, we're extended way longer than we've ever been. And so we continue to talk to our customers. That's why it's great to have the frame agreements and sort of the pipeline view beyond what's in the backlog. That's what we're using to plan with customers, and those orders are rolling to backlog at different times as we continue to move forward. RI and Prime Power projects, as I mentioned earlier, will also probably come in, in not a smooth sequential fashion. They'll be lumpy depending on when those orders get placed because they're typically big orders. So I think we'll continue to talk to our customers. And again, you can't just look at one metric, like backlog growth in a quarter or book-to-bill in a quarter. It has to be taken into context with continued momentum in sales to users, our ability to produce more and get more product out the door. There are a lot of things that we're watching on the health of the business, more than just book-to-bill and a singular backlog number.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Our next question comes from Kyle Menges at Citi.

passages.heading: Kyle Menges, Analyst, Citi
passages.text: Kyle Menges, Analyst, Citi: Great. I would love to hear from you guys how the landscape might be changing a little bit as far as the demand you're seeing in the data center market. Maybe you can talk a little bit about how you're seeing things evolve in demand for turbines versus natural gas reciprocating engines and then for diesel backup. And then also, as you're booking into the latter part of this decade and having a lot of discussions—it sounds like a lot of quoting activity to 2030 and even beyond—I would love to get just some sense of how you could see your mix shifting, maybe that mix of prime versus backup where you've been versus where that mix is heading as you look to 2030.

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO: Yes. As we talk to our customers, we've not seen really any change since the last quarter in our discussions with customers. We continue to see momentum in standby diesel backup, which has been the growing base of our business for quite a while before even really AI started to accelerate the growth even more, driven by a lot of demand for cloud compute, and AI has obviously accelerated that. When it comes to Prime Power versus diesel, that's one of the things that's good about the capacity we put in place: it's pretty fungible as long as we have line of sight to those orders. If you get the largest 3520, that one, they're probably a little more extended on the Gas 3520K. But keep in mind as well that the capacity we have in place and the momentum we have are about more than just power generation. We continue to see momentum there. Oil and gas, and I think we're going to move a lot of natural gas in the next few years, is really strong in gas compression, both at Solar Turbines and in our reciprocating engine business. Demand is there for that. Marine and large engines also go into our mining products, so as mining picks up, we're excited about making sure that we can serve those customers. And really, when you talk about all these other applications aside from diesel standby, as the field population grows, we need to be able to support customers in the aftermarket and grow services. So the capacity is all aligned to what we plan to have in

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: place to meet our goals in 2030.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: We'll go next to Kristen Owen at Oppenheimer.

passages.heading: Kristen Owen, Analyst, Oppenheimer
passages.text: Kristen Owen, Analyst, Oppenheimer: We've talked a lot about the synchronous growth within the portfolio, but I'm hoping you can maybe double-click for us on the construction side. You called out the tough comps here in the fourth quarter, but backlog growth in construction—can you maybe help us understand or give us some color on the underlying demand? How much of that growth is going into rental for your own fleet versus third parties, and maybe some of these other sources of demand outside of rental and megaprojects?

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO: Yes, we've seen really strong order rates and strong STUs continue in construction. So we're really excited about the progress we have there and the initiatives that we've announced. I think it's the seventh consecutive STU growth quarter, and we'll see as we move forward. But our goal and our strategy really are to get customers in the cabs of Cat machines, whether they want to rent, lease, or buy, and we're seeing customers do all three. We're really excited, and we were heavy in the fleet load in the Major Projects fleet in the third quarter. Basically, as soon as we can get fleet on the ground, they're moving to projects. So I think that's going to be a great initiative for us to continue to drive rental. And the point of that is to supplement. If you think about that strategy, the Major Projects JV supplements the local dealer where they wouldn't have the scale to get to projects before. So it drives not only Major Projects, but allows each of the individual dealers to be in more rental deals as they move forward as well. So we're seeing great progress there. We're excited about Cat Compact and how we're taking care of customers in the growing compact equipment industry. And in particular, we've seen large infrastructure projects, high IIJA spending that still has a lot of money left to be spent and projects left to be completed. I'm confident we'll continue to prioritize critical infrastructure as we move forward. Data centers obviously

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: have a little bit of a rollover into CI as well. And so we're seeing really good momentum with the CI team. We're getting closer to customers than we ever have, and it's showing in their results. And we're seeing strength in all three of our segments right now, which is really exciting.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: And today's final question comes from the line of Stephen Volkmann from Jefferies.

passages.heading: Stephen Volkmann, Analyst, Jefferies
passages.text: Stephen Volkmann, Analyst, Jefferies: Joe, I'm just wondering if you have any update on the 10-megawatt MaK restart that you're doing, and how we should think about that kind of ramping going forward?

passages.heading: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO
passages.text: Joseph Creed, Chairman and CEO: Yes, we plan to ship our first units here in the fourth quarter, and we'll continue to ramp as we go through next year on restarting the 10-megawatt MaK engine and using it in power generation. I think that's going to be a great opportunity for us as we move into—we'll get started here in the fourth quarter, but as we move into 2027. So everything is on track with that program. All right. Well, that was the last question. So I just want to say thanks for joining us today. We really appreciate your questions. And I'm really proud of our team, the Caterpillar team's strong performance in what's been a pretty dynamic environment as we try to ramp production, add capacity, and take care of our customers. We're well positioned to deliver a strong year, and we'll continue creating long-term value for our customers and shareholders. So thank you. I'll turn it back over to Alex.

passages.heading: Alex Kapper, Vice President of Investor Relations
passages.text: Alex Kapper, Vice President of Investor Relations: Thank you, Joe, Kyle, Stephanie, and everyone who joined us today. A replay of our call will be available online later this morning. We'll also post a transcript on our Investor Relations website as soon as it's available. You'll also find a third-quarter results video with our CFO and an SEC filing with our sales-to-users data. Visit investors.caterpillar.com and then click on Financials to view those materials. If you have any questions, please reach out to me or Ryan Coleman. The Investor Relations general phone number is (309) 675-4549. Now let's turn it back over to Audra to conclude our call.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Thank you. And that concludes our call. Thank you for joining. You may all now disconnect.

# Consolidated business results for six months of the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027 (U.S. GAAP)

October 29, 2026

Komatsu Ltd. today announced its consolidated business results for six months of the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027 (U.S. GAAP). The highlights are described below.

**1. Results for six months ended September 30, 2026**  
   
 For the first six-month period (April 1- September 30, 2026) of the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027, consolidated net sales totaled JPY 2,158.6 billion, an increase of 14.1% from the corresponding period a year ago. In the construction, mining and utility equipment business, sales increased from the corresponding period a year ago, supported by the depreciation of the Japanese yen compared to the corresponding period a year ago, increased sales volume and improved selling prices. In the industrial machinery and others business, sales increased from the corresponding period a year ago, mainly supported by increased sales for the semiconductor industry.

With respect to profits for the first six-month period under review in the construction, mining and utility equipment business, despite factors such as increased costs, profits increased primarily due to the Japanese yen's depreciation, improved selling prices and an increase in sales volume. In the retail finance and industrial machinery and others business, profits increased. As a result, operating income totaled JPY 286.6 billion, an increase of 3.5% from the corresponding period a year ago and the operating income ratio decreased by 1.3 percentage point from the corresponding period a year ago to 13.3%. Income before income taxes and equity in earnings of affiliated companies increased by 4.9% from the corresponding period a year ago to JPY 271.0 billion. Net income attributable to Komatsu Ltd. increased by 9.2% from the corresponding period a year ago to JPY 191.9 billion.  
  ![](/en/-/media/home/newsroom/2026/1029_1/eng1-1.jpg?h=855&w=986&rev=d800c6384ddd4daf969f1cf6e3186538&hash=E85DD8E5182FE04B3B275A2E0C0FB768)

**2. Projection for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027（FY2026）**

Komatsu has made upward revisions to its projected consolidated sales and profits for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027 from those announced on July 29. These revisions reflect stronger-than-expected demand across many regions in the construction, mining, and utility equipment business during the first six-month period, with demand expected to remain above initial expectations for the full year, as well as the greater-than-expected depreciation of the Japanese yen during the second quarter.  
   
 The average exchange rates assumed in the projection for the second six-month period remain unchanged from those announced on July 29, 2026 (USD 1=JPY 150.0, EUR 1=JPY 174.0, and AUD 1=JPY 106.0). With respect to average exchange rates for the full year, Komatsu now estimates them at USD 1=JPY 154.5, EUR 1=JPY 179.1, and AUD 1=JPY 109.2 (previous projections: USD 1=JPY 152.1, EUR 1=JPY 176.6, and AUD 1=JPY 107.6).
